transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-19
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Daniel Ruiz (CTO, Stratify Labs), Asha Raman (Lead ML Eng), Priya Kapoor (Platform Eng)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about 40 minutes, quick intros?
[00:05] Daniel: yeah daniel here, cto, we run a product analytics stack and are adding an llm layer for natural language queries over event data.
[00:10] Asha: hi i'm asha, lead ml, i'm owning the model integration work.
[00:15] Priya: priya platform, i'll be responsible for infra and security bits.
[00:20] Maya: thanks; liam from our side is the solutions engineer, he'll take the technical bits.
[00:25] Liam: hey everyone, quick agenda: figure out throughput/latency targets, budget constraints, and which deployment mode makes sense hosted vs dedicated vs private. also batching/caching levers and how that affects per-token economics.

[00:40] Daniel: to be upfront, we have a pretty tight operating budget for year one, about $120k annual for inference costs, and we need to support roughly 500 requests per second at peak, average prompt length ~300 tokens, generation ~150 tokens.
[00:50] Maya: great, good to know. just to clarify, 500 rps peak, 300 in, 150 out, so ~450 tokens total per request? is that right.
[00:55] Asha: roughly, yes, sometimes less, some queries are short, but that's a good baseline.

[01:10] Liam: ok doing quick math on the call: if you were on a 1st-party hosted per-token price of say $0.0003 per input token and $0.0004 per output token (example numbers), that would be 300*0.0003 + 150*0.0004 = 0.09 + 0.06 = $0.15 per request. at 500 rps sustained that's $75 / second, which is obviously too high monthly. so this is where batching and KV/prefix caching move the needle.
[01:30] Priya: can you explain the batching impact in simpler terms? our platform team is worried about latency for interactive queries.
[01:40] Liam: yep. two levers: batching across concurrent requests to increase GPU utilization and reduce per-token cost, and prefix/KV caching for repeated context—if many queries share the same event context or prompt prefix we can avoid re-computing the first N tokens. batching helps cost but increases tail latency if you wait for batch fills; Redwood supports micro-batching + strict latency SLOs and adaptive batching so you get modest batching without big latency spikes.
[02:10] Daniel: what kind of latency tradeoffs are we looking at? our SLO is 200ms p95 for short queries, and under 1s for longer ones.
[02:20] Liam: hosted small models can hit 100-300ms for short generation with small batch sizes. for your 450-token total workload, generation dominates. with our dedicated offering you can reserve capacity for predictable latency and higher batch sizes (so better cost) while keeping p95 ~ <700ms for many settings. private on-prem tends to have higher operational overhead but you get data residency control.

[02:50] Asha: curious about concrete numbers — can you show us examples where batching cut cost per token?
[02:55] Liam: yes, typical numbers we cite: unbatched throughput might be 1-2 tokens/sec/core cost-wise, with batching you can increase utilization 3-5x depending on model and sequence lengths. that translates to e.g., effective per-token cost reduction of 30-60% relative to pure on-demand. i'll include a spreadsheet with sample scenarios.
[03:20] Maya: also important: caching. if you have repeated prefixes — say the query always includes a common filter block or schema description — we can cache the kv state for that prefix so only the novel tokens are generated. that can drop your average token count per request significantly.
[03:35] Priya: we do have a lot of shared context — the same event schema and company metadata — how fast is cache warming and invalidation?
[03:40] Liam: cache warm is immediate after the first request hits the instance; invalidation is policy-driven — TTLs or on-change invalidations. if you have tens of thousands of unique prefixes you'll get less benefit; if there's a small set of common prefixes (even 50-200) you can save a lot.

[04:10] Daniel: okay but with our $120k budget what's realistic? we'd need a model of expected monthly costs.
[04:20] Maya: we'll put together a tailored cost model. high level options: hosted pay-as-you-go (no infra commits) often higher per-token but quick; dedicated reserved capacity lowers per-token and is good for predictable throughput; private gives max control but has platform licensing + infra cost. given your budget and 500 rps peaks, dedicated pilot is often best to validate.
[04:40] Asha: what's the typical committed spend for dedicated?
[04:45] Maya: it depends on the instance types and the model family. many of our mid-market customers start with a 6-12 month commit in the $150k-$400k range — but we can do a smaller dedicated pilot to validate throughput/costs for a quarter.
[04:58] Priya: is there a way to decouple control plane and data plane so we can keep data in our VPC but Redwood manages control plane?
[05:05] Liam: yes that's our Private deployment pattern — private control plane with VPC peering and customer-managed data plane. you can also do Hybrid where model inference runs in customer VPC while control plane is managed. we'll share compliance docs — SOC 2, encryption at rest, KMS integration.

[05:30] Daniel: i keep hearing per-token numbers — what's realistic per effective token after batching and caching?
[05:35] Liam: broad ranges: for open quantized models on dedicated infra you might get to $0.00002-$0.00006 per token effective after batching and caching for long-running workloads. hosted might be $0.00008-$0.00015 effective. again depends on model, quant, and utilization. for your mix i'd estimate a realistic hosted run-rate would be >$200k/year unless you aggressively cache/batch. dedicated pilot could bring that under $120k if hit utilization targets.
[06:05] Asha: how sensitive is that to prompt length distribution? if 20% of requests are long 1k+ tokens does that blow the budget?
[06:14] Liam: long tails matter. batching is less effective for very long sequences because they occupy GPU longer; caching helps only if long sequences share prefixes. we recommend sampling your real traffic and running an eval in our benchmark harness — that's the only way to be confident.

[06:40] Priya: from a network/security perspective, what's the egress pattern? do we need direct peering for low latency?
[06:45] Liam: for dedicated/private we colocate in region and support VPC peering, private endpoints, and direct connect for minimal hop latency. hosted public endpoints will have internet egress — fine for many use cases but for regulated data you'd pick private.

[07:10] Daniel: are there tooling levers to automatically choose cheaper model variants when tolerance for quality is present?

[07:15] Maya: yes our smart routing can fall back to smaller/quantized model variants based on policy (latency, cost, region). Redwood Optimize also recommends quantization profiles and batching configs by workload.

[07:30] Asha: ok, let's be practical: we want to run a 2-week pilot against a subset of traffic (maybe 10% of live) to capture real token distribution and run dedicated instances to see cost and latency. can you support that?
[07:40] Liam: absolutely. SE will set up the benchmark harness, we'll need a sample prompt set, traffic traces, and SLO targets. we'll run dedicated reserved instances for the pilot and produce a post-run cost/latency report.

[08:00] Priya: what data do you need from our side?
[08:05] Liam: sample prompt set (10k-50k samples preferred with distribution), traffic profile (rps over time, % short/long queries), any auth constraints for private endpoints, and security contacts.

[08:20] Maya: i'll follow up with a checklist and the pricing spreadsheet.

[08:25] Daniel: what about model updates/pinning? we want reproducible results for audits.
[08:30] Liam: you can pin model versions, we keep model artifacts in the registry and provide audit logs for inference calls. integration with KMS for key access and audit trails is standard.

[08:45] Asha: any quick wins you recommend to reduce costs before a pilot?
[08:50] Liam: yes: 1) identify common prefixes for kv caching, 2) shorten prompts where possible and move static context to embeddings or external memory, 3) enable micro-batching with strict latency targets, 4) pick a quantized model family for inference.

[09:10] Maya: recap and next steps: we'll send the pricing + batching models spreadsheet, SOC2/compliance docs, and an SE-run pilot proposal. action items on the doc — liam will run initial throughput estimates, asha/priya to provide prompt samples, maya to send pricing.

[09:30] Daniel: sounds good, thanks everyone. we'll aim to get the samples to you by friday.

[09:35] Maya: great talk soon. bye.

(end of transcript)
